title: Token boundary caching & ephemeral thread heuristics – sketchpad
content:
Purpose
-------
This doc captures ideas, observations and quick experiments around two related CPU-side bottlenecks we keep seeing in small/short requests: 1) repeated token boundary scanning (esp for long prefix reuse across requests), and 2) scheduling overhead from ephemeral worker threads / threadpool handoffs in Python-heavy request paths. Goal is to capture low-effort mitigations, measurement plan, and a few microbenchmarks to validate changes before larger refactors.

Background / motivation
-----------------------
Symptoms observed in production traces:
- 95th/99th p95 spikes on 50–200 token requests where GPU time is tiny compared to host CPU preproc.
- Flamegraphs repeatedly show small, hot loops in tokenizer boundary detection and many short-lived stack frames around thread handoffs / queue popping.
- Sampling during busy minutes shows a steady ~10–20% CPU consumed by request preparse/token boundary checks even when payloads are short.
- Previous mitigations (fast parse heuristics, JSON pre-parse) reduced but did not eliminate the noise.

Hypotheses
----------
H1: A lot of token boundary work is duplicated across requests with similar prefixes (same customer prompts / system prompts) -> caching prefix token boundary results (e.g. offset tables or segment-level tokenization metadata) will reduce CPU and avoid rescanning text.
H2: Ephemeral threads / per-request worker handoffs (we create or wake many short tasks) create scheduling latency and syscalls (futex/wakeup) that dominate at low token counts. Moving to a cooperative work-stealing ring / pinned long-lived workers or batching small tasks to a single worker reduces tail latency.
H3: Python-side object churn during tokenization (temporary lists, small-string slicing) increases GC and increases latency variability. Lightweight in-place buffer views or C-level buffer-sharing reduces the impact.

Measurements to collect (what to instrument)
-------------------------------------------
- Tokenization microprofile (per-request): number of scans, bytes scanned, boundary checks, cache hits/misses.
- Syscall counts and futex wakeups per request during preproc path.
- Python allocation counts and GC frequency during hot loops.
- End-to-end latency broken down: request-parse, tokenization, routing, GPU-init, kernel.
- Distribution by request length, by route, and by tenant.

Quick experiments (local / canary)
---------------------------------
Experiment A: Prefix token boundary cache (in-memory LRU keyed by sha256(prefix_text) + model/tokenizer version)
- Impl notes: cache stores vector of (byte_offset -> token_start_index) for every 4KB segment; on cache hit, tokenization resumes with O(1) mapping instead of rescanning entire prefix.
- Safety: TTL 5 minutes; max entries 10k; memory cap 200MB. Evict on memory pressure.
- Metrics: cache_hits, cache_misses, avg_bytes_scanned per request, CPU ms saved.
- Run: compare canary vs control for 48 hours on low-traffic region.

Experiment B: Sticky worker pool for short jobs (cohort < 200 tokens)
- Impl notes: maintain small fixed-size pool of long-lived workers pinned to cores (or core-affinity hints). Use a lock-free MPSC queue to push tasks. Workers process many tasks sequentially, amortizing wake/futex cost.
- Fallback: if queue full, route to general pool.
- Metrics: futex_wakeups_per_req, worker_cycle_utilization, tail latency p95/p99.
- Run: A/B test on synthetic short-request load then canary.

Experiment C: Tokenization buffer view API (reduce Python copies)
- Impl notes: expose tokenizer API that accepts memoryview/bytearray and returns token indices without creating intermediate strings. Add Cython wrapper for critical path.
- Metrics: Python allocations per req, GC pause time.

Microbenchmarks (commands and rough expected gains)
---------------------------------------------------
- baseline: wrk-like harness sending 1000 rps of 80-token requests (mix of short and short+prefix). measure cpu and latency.
- harness: python bench/tokenize_bench.py --rps 1000 --payload sample_prefixes.json
- expectation: prefix cache should reduce tokenization CPU by ~35–60% on reused prefixes; sticky worker pool reduces tail latency by 20–40% for p95/p99 under the synthetic microbench. Buffer API reduces Python allocs ~60%.

Sample microprofile snippets (representative)
-------------------------------------------
- tokenization.c:line 412 -> check_boundary (hot): 18%
- py_worker_handoff: futex_wait -> futex_wake: 12%
- json_parse_many_small: 6%
- heap_alloc_small_objects: 10%

Telemetry / schema additions
---------------------------
- Add tokenization.detail.* metrics: scans, bytes_scanned, cache_key, cache_hit (bool), segments_used (int).
- Add scheduling.futex_wakeups, scheduling.worker_lifetime_tasks.
- Add python.alloc_count, python.gc_pause_ms.

Implementation plan & priority
------------------------------
1) Low-friction: add lightweight prefix cache in tokenizer (no runtime-internal API changes). Small rollout flags and TTL. (owner: Priya) (ETA: 1 week prototype, 2 week canary)
2) Parallel: implement sticky worker pool as opt-in routing policy for short requests. (owner: Evan) (ETA: 3 weeks for prototype)
3) Buffer API + Cython wrapper: longer effort, requires careful safety checks. (owner: Mateo) (ETA: 4–6 weeks)
4) If wins are large, consider merging into platform default and exposing config in route settings.

Risks / open questions
----------------------
- Cache coherency: using an LRU TTL may be fine, but how to handle dynamic tokenizer changes or model upgrades? Need invalidation hooks from model rollouts.
- Memory vs CPU tradeoff: caching segments for many tenants could blow memory; need per-tenant caps or shared cache with eviction weighting.
- Affinity/pinning tradeoffs: pinning to cores harms binpacking on multi-tenant hosts. Maybe use soft affinity and cooperative scheduling instead.
- Do we need tenant-aware sizing? heavy tenants could monopolize sticky pools. Use fair-queueing across tenants.

Data collection checklist before starting canary
---------------------------------------------
- [ ] Add tokenization.detail telemetry and schema to metrics pipeline
- [ ] Implement lightweight experiment flags + config toggle per route
- [ ] Synthetic harness for short-request workloads and replay tool for historical prefixes
- [ ] Heatmap of tenants by short-request frequency (to size pools)
- [ ] Define safety knobs (max mem, TTL, fallback)

Notes / ad-hoc observations from quick local runs
------------------------------------------------
- With prefix cache enabled on local toy tokenizer, observed median tokenization time drop from 2.1ms -> 0.9ms on reused prefixes (sample set).
- Sticky worker prototype (pthread pinned) reduced futexs on local loopback by ~70% for 1k rps synthetic run but increased 50% CPU usage on the pinned core (expected).
- Cython buffer-view wrapper cut Python allocs per tokenization by ~45% in a minimal harness.

Next steps (immediate)
---------------------
- Sync with SRE/placement team about core-pinning policy (Mateo)
- Add minimal prefix cache POC as feature-flagged change (Priya)
- Prepare synthetic harness and run at 200–1000 rps to collect baseline (Evan)
- Schedule 30-minute sync to review telemetry schema and rollout safety (invite: eng-serving-runtime, eng-sre, product-hosted-api)

Appendix: quick pseudocode for prefix cache lookup
---------------------------------------------------
- key = sha256(prefix_text + tokenizer_version)
- entry = cache.get(key)
  if entry:
    for each segment in entry.segments:
      if request_bytes falls inside segment.range:
         map offset->token_idx from segment.index_table
         resume tokenization at token_idx
  else:
    scan as usual, build segments for first N KB, insert into cache

(we store coarse-grained index per 512–4096 bytes to bound memory; fine-tune segment size)
